sections.title: Warm-up
sections.lede: Read aloud and listen for the person who receives something.
sections.prompt: Say these sentences aloud. In each one, someone is helped, thanked or pleased.
items: Ich danke dir für die Hilfe.

sections.title: Learning objectives
sections.lede: By the end of this lesson you will be able to do these things.

sections.title: The big picture
sections.lede: The dative marks the person something is done for, given to or said to.

blocks.text: The dative is the case of the indirect object: the person who receives something or benefits from an action. It is also the case required by a group of very common verbs and by a small set of prepositions. You find it by asking Wem? — to whom?

items: Definite articles: dem (masculine), der (feminine), dem (neuter), den + -n (plural).
Indefinite articles: einem, einer, einem, and keinen + -n in the plural.
The pronoun changes too: mich becomes mir, dich becomes dir.
The dative plural adds -n to the noun unless the plural already ends in -n or -s: mit den Kindern, mit den Autos.
A few masculine nouns also add -n in the dative: dem Nachbarn, dem Kollegen.

blocks.title: Word order stays familiar
blocks.text: The dative object normally comes after the verb, just like an accusative object. Ich helfe dem Mann is the same shape as Ich sehe den Mann.

sections.title: Rules & patterns
sections.lede: Three tables cover most of the dative you will need at A2.

items: Dative verbs: helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, passen, schmecken, antworten, gratulieren, folgen.
Dative prepositions: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu.
Contractions are common: zu dem → zum, zu der → zur, bei dem → beim, von dem → vom.
Some masculine nouns add -n in the dative: dem Nachbarn, dem Kollegen, dem Studenten.

blocks.title: Memory hook
blocks.text: Think of the dative as the “give” case. If you can imagine handing something to the person, or doing something for them, the dative is likely.

sections.title: Vocabulary
sections.lede: These verbs and nouns appear with the dative again and again.

items.example: Ich danke dir für die Hilfe.
items.exampleEn: I thank you for the help.

sections.title: Example sentences
sections.lede: Every sentence contains a dative form. Find it before you read the note.

items.note: helfen takes the dative: mir, not mich.

items.de: Ich danke dir für deine Hilfe.
items.en: I thank you for your help.
items.note: danken takes the dative; für takes the accusative, so deine Hilfe stays accusative.

items.de: Das Geschenk gefällt meiner Mutter sehr.
items.en: My mother really likes the gift.
items.note: gefallen takes the dative: meiner Mutter. The gift is the subject.

items.de: Wir fahren mit dem Bus zum Bahnhof.
items.en: We are going to the station by bus.
items.note: mit and zu always take the dative; zum = zu dem.

items.de: Sie wohnt seit einem Jahr bei ihren Eltern.
items.en: She has been living with her parents for a year.
items.note: seit and bei take the dative; the plural noun keeps its -n.

sections.title: Pronunciation
sections.lede: Short dative pronouns are easy to swallow. Give them full value.

items.hint: Long ee, then a soft vowel-like r: meer. Do not reduce it to “ma”.
Long ee as well: deer. Keep it distinct from der.
Long ee followed by m: eem. It sounds close to ihm in Ihnen.
Short open ä and a clear double l: ge-FELT.
The ch after a is the rough sound of Bach, then a short second syllable: NAHKH-bar.

blocks.text: German often puts the person in the dative when describing a sensation or a state: Mir ist kalt, Mir ist schlecht, Mir geht es gut. English uses “I am cold” or “I feel sick”, with the person as subject; German presents the sensation as happening to the person.
The same pattern explains Wie geht es dir? and the formal Wie geht es Ihnen? The question is literally “how is it going to you?”, and the answer keeps the dative: Danke, mir geht es gut.

sections.title: Dialogue in context
sections.lede: A wardrobe has to get through a doorway.
sections.setting: In the hallway of an apartment building

lines.speaker: Frau Yilmaz
lines.de: Guten Tag, Herr Braun. Können Sie mir kurz helfen?
lines.en: Good day, Mr Braun. Can you help me for a moment?

lines.speaker: Herr Braun
lines.en: Of course. What is going on?

lines.speaker: Frau Yilmaz
lines.de: Der Schrank passt nicht durch die Tür. Mein Sohn braucht ihn für sein Zimmer.
lines.en: The wardrobe does not fit through the door. My son needs it for his room.

lines.speaker: Herr Braun
lines.en: No problem. I will help you.

lines.speaker: Frau Yilmaz
lines.de: Vielen Dank! Das gefällt meinem Sohn sicher.
lines.en: Many thanks! My son will certainly like that.

lines.speaker: Herr Braun
lines.en: So the wardrobe belongs to him?

lines.speaker: Frau Yilmaz
lines.de: Ja, er hat lange dafür gespart.
lines.en: Yes, he saved up for it for a long time.

lines.speaker: Herr Braun
lines.en: Then we will carry it together.

sections.title: Grammar spotlight
sections.heading: Wem? — finding the dative object
sections.lede: Ask Wem? instead of Wen? and the article changes.

items: In the dative, masculine and neuter share dem; feminine is der; plural is den plus -n on the noun.
The indefinite article follows the same pattern: einem, einer, einem, keinen + -n.
The pronoun mir is both “to me” and the dative in phrases such as Mir ist kalt.
Verbs like helfen, danken, gefallen, gehören, passen and schmecken never take a direct accusative object.

blocks.title: Weak masculine nouns
blocks.text: Nouns such as der Nachbar, der Kollege and der Student add -n or -en in the dative and accusative: dem Nachbarn, den Kollegen, den Studenten.

sections.tip: When you learn a new verb, learn its case at the same time. Write helfen + Dativ on the card, not just helfen = to help.

exercises.explanation: helfen takes the dative, and der Mann becomes dem Mann.

exercises.prompt: Complete the formal question: Wie geht es ___?
exercises.explanation: The formal dative pronoun is Ihnen. dir is informal.
gefallen takes the dative, so “I like it” is Es gefällt mir.

exercises.prompt: Which preposition always takes the dative?
exercises.explanation: mit is one of the dative prepositions: mit dem Bus. für, ohne and gegen take the accusative.
der Bus is masculine, and the dative of der is dem.
die Lehrerin is feminine, and the dative of die is der.
die Mutter is feminine, so mein becomes meiner in the dative.

exercises.prompt: Wir wohnen seit ___ Jahr in Berlin. (a)
exercises.explanation: das Jahr is neuter: seit einem Jahr.

exercises.prompt: Ich danke ___ für die Hilfe. (you, informal)

exercises.explanation: der Nachbar is masculine and takes the dative dem; the noun also adds -n.
das Fahrrad is neuter, and the dative of das is dem.

sections.title: Build the sentence
sections.lede: Build each sentence and keep the dative object after the verb.

exercises.explanation: A yes/no question starts with the verb; mir is the dative object and the infinitive is last.
Das Geschenk is the subject; meiner Mutter is the dative object.

exercises.prompt: Build: “I thank you for your help.”
exercises.answer: Ich danke dir für deine Hilfe.
exercises.explanation: dir is dative because of danken; für takes the accusative, so deine Hilfe.

exercises.prompt: Build: “We are going to the station by bus.”
exercises.answer: Wir fahren mit dem Bus zum Bahnhof.
exercises.explanation: mit dem Bus and zum Bahnhof are both dative phrases.

sections.title: Listening
sections.lede: Listen twice, then answer from memory.
sections.speaker: A neighbour on the phone

script.speaker: Frau Klein
script.de: Hallo Tom, hier ist Frau Klein. Hast du kurz Zeit?
script.en: Hello Tom, this is Mrs Klein. Do you have a moment?

script.speaker: Tom
script.de: Ja, natürlich. Was kann ich für Sie tun?
script.en: Yes, of course. What can I do for you?

script.speaker: Frau Klein
script.de: Kannst du mir morgen beim Umzug helfen?
script.en: Can you help me with the move tomorrow?

script.speaker: Tom
script.de: Klar. Wann brauchst du mich denn?
script.en: Sure. When do you need me, then?

script.speaker: Frau Klein
script.de: Um neun. Mein Bruder bringt den Transporter.
script.en: At nine. My brother is bringing the van.

script.speaker: Tom
script.de: Gut. Ich bringe meinen Freund mit. Er hilft dir auch.
script.en: Good. I will bring my friend along. He will help you too.

questions.explanation: She asks: Kannst du mir morgen beim Umzug helfen? — beim Umzug means with the move.

questions.prompt: When does Tom need to be there?
questions.explanation: She says: Um neun — at nine.
She says: Mein Bruder bringt den Transporter.

sections.title: Speaking
sections.lede: Politeness in German runs on the dative.
sections.prompt: Ask a stranger for help and thank them. Use at least three dative forms and one dative preposition.

model.de: Entschuldigung, können Sie mir bitte helfen? Ich suche den Bahnhof. Können Sie mir den Weg zeigen? Vielen Dank, das ist sehr freundlich von Ihnen. Ich danke Ihnen für die Hilfe.
model.en: Excuse me, can you help me, please? I am looking for the station. Can you show me the way? Many thanks, that is very kind of you. I thank you for your help.

tips: Use Ihnen with strangers and dir with friends. Mixing them sounds either rude or oddly intimate.
Keep the dative pronoun right after the verb: Können Sie mir helfen?
Remember that danken, helfen and gefallen never take mich, dich or ihn.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.lede: Accusative pronouns slip in easily. Check the verb first.

items.why: helfen requires the dative, so mich becomes mir.
danken takes the dative: ich danke dir.
gefallen takes the dative. The thing that pleases is the subject; the person is the dative object.
der Bus is masculine, and the dative of der is dem.

sections.title: Lesson assessment
sections.lede: Ten questions on dative articles, pronouns and verbs. Score 70% or more to pass.

questions.explanation: das Kind is neuter, and the dative of das is dem.

questions.prompt: Complete the informal question: Wie geht es ___?
questions.explanation: The informal dative pronoun is dir; Ihnen is the formal form.
schmecken takes the dative: Das Essen schmeckt mir.

questions.prompt: Which preposition always takes the dative?
questions.explanation: nach is a dative preposition: nach dem Essen. für, ohne and um take the accusative.

questions.prompt: Ich danke ___ für das Geschenk. (you, informal)

questions.explanation: bei takes the dative, and the plural dative of ihr is ihren.
der Zug is masculine, so the dative article is dem.
Verb first in a yes/no question, dative mir after the subject, infinitive last.
The gift is the subject; the person who likes it stands in the dative.

questions.prompt: Build: “I thank you for your help.”
questions.answer: Ich danke dir für deine Hilfe.
questions.explanation: danken takes the dative dir; für takes the accusative deine Hilfe.
